extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / creative writers (novelists, short-story writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting realistic, purposeful dialogue in fiction that reveals character, advances plot, and maintains reader engagement. Covers functions dialogue must serve, style and tag conventions, formatting, common failure modes, and quality indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move the story forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should advance the plot or scene movement rather than merely fill space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each line of dialogue must serve at least one functional purpose; if it doesn't change circumstances or decisions, consider cutting or rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character (voice, attitude, hidden self)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should disclose aspects of a character's personality, attitudes, or concealed motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distinct word choice, rhythm, and subtext to show who a character is rather than stating it outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey information
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue may communicate necessary facts to the reader or other characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious or clunky exposition; integrate needed information naturally and sparingly so it still feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create or release tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should build, sustain, or relieve dramatic tension in a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use withholding, interruptions, or subtext to generate tension; allow moments of release to alter pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish relationship dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should indicate power, intimacy, distance, or other relational qualities between speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word choice, address forms, interruptions, and who speaks when all signal relationship dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each character sounds different
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must have distinct vocabulary, rhythm, and speech patterns so they are distinguishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two characters sound identical, consider conflating them or sharpening their distinct voices through diction, sentence length, and idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut conversational filler
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove filler words and phrases like 'um,' 'uh,' 'I mean,' and excessive greetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim or omit hesitations and scaffolding that add no dramatic value; for phone calls, begin after the initial 'Hello.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Short sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor short, punchy lines over long speeches; people rarely deliver extended monologues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break longer ideas into shorter lines or mixes of speech and beats to maintain realism and pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real isn't realistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribing real speech verbatim often reads poorly on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest realistic speech rather than fully transcribing it: capture the impression of how people talk without reproducing every nonessential utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accent/dialect sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid heavy phonetic spelling to render dialect; it can alienate readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imply accent via vocabulary, syntax, and brief markers rather than sustained misspellings or apostrophe-storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtext over text
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should often not say exactly what they mean; imply motivations and feelings beneath speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use what is left unsaid, contradictions between speech and action, and indirectness to create depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'said' almost always (invisible tag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the neutral tag 'said' so the tag doesn't call attention to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Said' recedes from the reader's attention; avoid flashy synonyms that draw focus away from the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adverbs on tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not modify speech tags with adverbs like 'she said softly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show tone through verb choice (e.g., 'she whispered') or through action beats rather than adverbial tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action beats instead of tags when natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ short actions that accompany speech to identify speakers and add context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'She set the cup down. "I don't think so."' Action beats can replace tags and convey emotion or movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't always tag
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit tags in rapid back-and-forth between two named speakers to benefit pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When speaker identity is clear, untagged exchanges can quicken rhythm and enhance realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: New speaker = new paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin a new paragraph each time the speaker changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard formatting rule preserves clarity of who is speaking and is essential for readable dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks in American English and single in British English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent with your regional convention throughout the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation inside quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place punctuation (commas, periods, question marks, etc.) inside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard punctuation rules for quoted speech to avoid distracting errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em-dash for interruption; ellipsis for trailing-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an em-dash to indicate an interrupted line and an ellipsis for a trailing-off thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mark that matches the intent: interruption (—) versus hesitation or fade-out (...).

rubrics_metrics.name: "As you know, Bob" (info-dump through dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters telling each other things they both already know to convey information to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived exposition; find more natural ways to reveal facts or restructure scenes so information is discovered rather than told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches on the writer's themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters delivering long speeches that mouth the author's themes rather than arising from character or situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let themes emerge from action and conflict; avoid using dialogue as a soapbox for authorial views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive greetings, goodbyes, or polite formulas that add nothing to the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim social scaffolding unless it serves a character or plot function.

rubrics_metrics.name: All characters sound like the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' voices reflecting the writer's voice rather than their own distinct perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to inhabit different characters distinctly through vocabulary, cadence, and perspective; read dialogue aloud in each character's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialect via apostrophe-storm
rubrics_metrics.description: Overuse of apostrophes and altered spellings to represent dialect (e.g., 'goin' for 'going').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy phonetic spellings; they can be hard to read and can caricature characters unintentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag adverb soup
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-reliance on adverbial tags (e.g., 'sighed sadly,' 'exclaimed loudly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how something is said through verb choice, action beats, or the dialogue content itself instead of piling adverbs onto tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names overused in address
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive repetition of a character's name in dialogue (e.g., 'Tom, would you, Tom, like...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use names naturally; constant repetition reads awkward and can signal poor characterization or an attempt to indicate who's speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue is overheard (sounds like real people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good dialogue reads as if the reader is overhearing a natural exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the believable suggestive quality of real speech rather than literal transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct voices identifiable without tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character's voice should be recognizable even when tags are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by removing tags and seeing if the speakers remain clear; strengthen diction and rhythm accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension/withholding present
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective dialogue includes withholding information or emotional restraint that creates stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subtext, evasions, and partial disclosures to keep readers engaged and curious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtext readable
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying meaning or motivation beneath characters' words should be perceivable to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer speech with implications, contradictions between words and actions, and contextual cues that reveal deeper intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action beats integrated with speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical actions tied to dialogue should be blended into the exchange to enrich scene and identify speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tagging every line; use beats to show movement, emotion, and to break up speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing alternates exchanges and silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Good scenes balance rapid back-and-forth with pauses and silence to control rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary line length, include beats and moments of silence to shape tempo and tension.
